title: CHAPTER 14: ECONOMIC PLANNING & FIVE-YEAR PLANS IN INDIA

blocks.content: PART A: THE BASIC ECONOMIC PROBLEM AND NEED FOR PLANNING

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Economic planning in India was adopted post-independence to tackle resource scarcity and promote systematic growth.
The First Five-Year Plan focused heavily on agriculture, while the Second Plan prioritized heavy industries under the Mahalanobis Model.
Continuous planning faced interruptions during the Plan Holidays (1966–69) and the Rolling Plan (1978–80).
The Planning Commission was replaced by NITI Aayog in 2015 to adopt a bottom-up approach to national development.

blocks.content: All economies face the problem of scarcity. Human wants are unlimited, but resources such as land, labour, capital, entrepreneurship and technology are limited. Because resources are scarce, choices must be made regarding their use.

This scarcity gives rise to three basic economic questions:

• What goods and services should be produced?

• How should these goods and services be produced?

• For whom should these goods and services be produced?

In a free market economy, these questions are answered automatically by the price mechanism, which operates through demand, supply and profit motive. However, market forces often fail to ensure social justice, equitable distribution and long-term development.
Economic planning represents a conscious effort by the state to guide economic activity in a socially desirable direction.
PART B: MEANING, NATURE AND SCOPE OF ECONOMIC PLANNING

Economic planning is a deliberate and systematic effort by the government to control, guide and regulate the allocation of resources according to predetermined national priorities to achieve specific economic and social objectives within a fixed time period.
Planning involves setting clear targets, estimating available resources, prioritising sectors, allocating financial and physical resources, implementing policies and continuously monitoring progress.

Economic planning has the following characteristics:

• It is goal-oriented and future-focused

• It is comprehensive in scope

• It is time-bound

• It is government-led

• It emphasises social welfare rather than private profit

The scope of economic planning extends to all major sectors of the economy, including agriculture, industry, services, infrastructure, employment, poverty alleviation, education, health, regional development and environmental sustainability.
PART C: WHY INDIA ADOPTED ECONOMIC PLANNING
6. Economic Conditions at the Time of Independence

At the time of independence in 1947, India inherited an underdeveloped and stagnant economy. Per capita income was extremely low, poverty was widespread, unemployment was high, agriculture was backward, industries were poorly developed, and infrastructure such as roads, power and irrigation was inadequate.
There also existed sharp regional imbalances and extreme inequality in income and wealth.
7. Inadequacy of Market Forces in India

The market mechanism alone could not address India’s development challenges. Private investment was insufficient, profit motives discouraged investment in social sectors, and market forces could not ensure equitable growth.
Therefore, state intervention through economic planning was considered essential.
PART D: FEATURES AND OBJECTIVES OF ECONOMIC PLANNING

• Existence of a central planning authority

• Clearly defined national objectives

• Planning for a fixed time horizon

• Optimal utilisation of scarce resources

• Emphasis on social justice and welfare

• Coordination between different sectors of the economy

Economic Growth: Achieving a sustained increase in national income and per capita income.



Employment Generation: Creating sufficient job opportunities to absorb the growing labour force.



Poverty Alleviation: Improving the standard of living of the poor and vulnerable sections.



Reduction of Inequality: Ensuring a more equitable distribution of income and wealth.



Balanced Regional Development: Reducing disparities between developed and backward regions.



Self-Reliance: Reducing dependence on foreign countries for essential goods and capital.
PART E: TYPES AND MODELS OF ECONOMIC PLANNING
CHAPTER 14: ECONOMIC PLANNING & FIVE-YEAR PLANS IN INDIA

Centralised Planning involves decision-making by a central authority.



Decentralised Planning involves participation of state and local governments.



Democratic Planning operates within a democratic political framework.



Indicative Planning provides guidelines to the private sector rather than commands.

Mahalanobis Model emphasised heavy industries and capital goods sector.



Agriculture-based Model focused on food security and rural development.



Mixed Economy Model allowed coexistence of public and private sectors.
PART F: PLANNING INSTITUTIONS IN INDIA
The Planning Commission was established in 1950. It was responsible for formulating Five-Year Plans, assessing national resources, allocating plan outlays and monitoring implementation.

blocks.content: PART H: ACHIEVEMENTS AND LIMITATIONS OF PLANNING
Economic planning contributed to industrialisation, infrastructure development, poverty reduction, scientific and technological progress, and greater self-reliance.
Despite achievements, planning suffered from inefficiency, bureaucratic delays, persistent inequality, unemployment and fiscal stress.
PART I: TRANSITION TO NITI AAYOG
In 2015, the Planning Commission was replaced by NITI Aayog, which functions as a policy think-tank and promotes cooperative federalism and long-term strategic planning.

• Economic planning is state-directed development

• Five-Year Plans guided India’s economic transformation

• Planning Commission was replaced by NITI Aayog

• Inclusive and sustainable growth is the modern objective
